articles.title: Democrat Abdul El-Sayed claims victory in Michigan Senate battle
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: El-Sayed won despite a last-minute hiccup in his campaign when congresswoman Haley Stevens, who lost the Democratic primary, came out in support of Rogers at the 11th hour

Democrat Abdul El-Sayed said early on Wednesday (November 4, 2026) that he had won a US Senate seat in Michigan over former Republican lawmaker Mike Rogers, which would make him the first Muslim elected to the upper chamber of Congress.
“Michigan, we did it!” Mr. El-Sayed said in a speech at his election headquarters in Detroit.
“I am so proud and honored to stand here as your senator-elect from the great state of Michigan.”
Mr. El-Sayed won despite a last-minute hiccup in his campaign when congresswoman Haley Stevens, who lost the Democratic primary to El-Sayed, came out in support of Rogers at the 11th hour.
The Michigan doctor rallied voters on leftist campaign promises, including universal health care, to hold a key U.S. Senate seat for Democrats, taking over from the retiring Gary Peters.
Republicans ran a scorched-earth campaign to paint Democrats as communists and branded Mr. El-Sayed a terrorist who would endanger Americans.
But the straight-talking 42-year-old El-Sayed pledged to help cash-strapped voters navigate America’s thorny health care system.
“You deserve to be able to see a doctor without getting a huge bill,” he told Michiganders on the eve of the vote, vowing to upend America’s divisive multi-billion-dollar for-profit medical system.
During the race, Mr. El-Sayed drew huge campaign crowds across the state, even in deeply conservative Republican areas.
Mr. El-Sayed also vowed to get “money out of politics” and address the harsh economic woes that have voters yearning for a political newcomer to shake up the status quo.

El-Sayed won despite a last-minute hiccup in his campaign when congresswoman Haley Stevens, who lost the Democratic primary, came out in support of Rogers at the 11th hour

Democrat Abdul El-Sayed said early on Wednesday (November 4, 2026) that he had won a US Senate seat in Michigan over former Republican lawmaker Mike Rogers, which would make him the first Muslim elected to the upper chamber of Congress.

“Michigan, we did it!” Mr. El-Sayed said in a speech at his election headquarters in Detroit.

“I am so proud and honored to stand here as your senator-elect from the great state of Michigan.”

Mr. El-Sayed won despite a last-minute hiccup in his campaign when congresswoman Haley Stevens, who lost the Democratic primary to El-Sayed, came out in support of Rogers at the 11th hour.

The Michigan doctor rallied voters on leftist campaign promises, including universal health care, to hold a key U.S. Senate seat for Democrats, taking over from the retiring Gary Peters.

Republicans ran a scorched-earth campaign to paint Democrats as communists and branded Mr. El-Sayed a terrorist who would endanger Americans.

But the straight-talking 42-year-old El-Sayed pledged to help cash-strapped voters navigate America’s thorny health care system.

“You deserve to be able to see a doctor without getting a huge bill,” he told Michiganders on the eve of the vote, vowing to upend America’s divisive multi-billion-dollar for-profit medical system.

During the race, Mr. El-Sayed drew huge campaign crowds across the state, even in deeply conservative Republican areas.

Mr. El-Sayed also vowed to get “money out of politics” and address the harsh economic woes that have voters yearning for a political newcomer to shake up the status quo.

Every single graduate of her high school earned admission to college, despite 86 per cent of them living in low-income households.

articles.title: Court grants bail to driver of bus in Bhandup accident case
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: The Bombay High Court has granted bail to Santosh Sawant, driver of a bus of BEST, in the Bhandup station accident case in which four persons died and 12 persons suffered injuries.

The court said the defence argument had substance at the stage of bail: Sawant may not have received training that BEST requires to operate a bus that runs on electricity. Justice Shyam Chandak made the observation while granting bail.

The court took note of a letter that a depot manager of BEST sent to the police on January 7. The letter stated that the undertaking did not have a certificate that confirmed whether Sawant had received training to drive a bus that runs on electricity. The name of Sawant was not on the list of drivers who had training. BEST assigned Sawant to operate a bus on Route 606 from December 1, 2025, even though the name of Sawant was not on the list.
The prosecution alleged that Sawant drove the bus at speed and without care when the bus went out of control near Bhandup railway station (West). The bus hit pedestrians who stood near a bus stop.

Devendra Patil, lawyer for Sawant, argued that BEST assigned Sawant to drive a bus that runs on electricity although Sawant had not undergone training. The defence submitted that refusal of the assignment could have led to action under discipline rules and to loss of job. It was brought to the notice of the court that there was no evidence that Sawant drove the bus at speed on purpose or that Sawant was under the influence of alcohol or drugs.
The court considered that Sawant had worked with BEST since 2011 and had no record of an accident. The court also noted that the trial may not conclude soon and that the case lists 56 witnesses.

Sawant had approached the High Court after the Sessions Court rejected the bail plea of Sawant. Sawant has been in jail for 11 months since the arrest of Sawant. The court accepted the argument of Sawant and granted bail to him.

articles.title: Congress slams dilution of grievance redressal rules under rural jobs scheme
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: Dropping of key accountability provisions is just another step towards reducing a “rights-based” law into an administrative scheme, says Congress leader Jairam Ramesh

Criticising the government for weakening the grievance redressal mechanism under the rural employment programme Viksit Bharat Guarantee for Rozgar and Aajeevika Mission (Gramin), which replaced the Mahatma Gandhi National Employment Guarantee Act in July this year, Congress general secretary (communications) Jairam Ramesh said the government has reduced India’s most significant rights-based law to an administrative scheme.

Mr. Ramesh was responding to The Hindu’s report on the government dropping several provisions that had figured in the draft rules circulated in May, some of which were also part of the previous rural jobs programme.

Key clauses dropped include a provision requiring the registration of a first information report (FIR) for prima facie evidence of financial irregularities, and the requirement to place action-taken reports before local body meetings for review and monitoring.

In a post on X , Mr. Ramesh said that while the government had an opportunity to strengthen mechanisms to address violations of the programme’s provisions, it had instead “removed those avenues altogether”.

In the continuing trend of converting India's most significant rights-based law into nothing more than an administrative scheme, the Union Ministry of Rural Development (MoRD) has notified a set of rules on grievance redress which further disempower workers and people, leaving their so called right as yet another jumla. Where the Government could have shown its intent to immediately redress violations of the core provisions of the Act, it has decided to remove those avenues altogether. The final VB–G RAM G Grievance Redressal Rules, notified by MoRD on 2 November 2026, have significantly diluted several important provisions contained in the draft Rules published in May 2026. The key changes are: 1.⁠ ⁠Removal of penalties for failure to resolve grievances within the stipulated timeframe: The draft Rules explicitly stated that failure to dispose of a grievance within seven working days would constitute a contravention of the Act and attract action under Section 27. This provision has been deleted from the final Rules. While timelines remain, there is no longer an explicit provision in the Rules holding officials accountable for non-compliance. 2.⁠ ⁠Removal of the obligation to initiate criminal proceedings in cases of financial irregularities: The draft required the District Programme Coordinator (DPC), after obtaining legal advice, to ensure that an FIR was lodged and necessary proceedings initiated where prima facie evidence of financial irregularities emerged from preliminary enquiries or social audit findings. This provision has been entirely deleted. 3.⁠ ⁠Removal of mandatory oversight by elected Panchayati Raj Institutions: The draft required action taken on grievances to be placed before Intermediate and District Panchayat meetings for review and monitoring. This provision has been deleted, weakening democratic oversight of grievance redressal. 4.⁠ ⁠Removal of mandatory weekly grievance-receiving days: The draft required officials at every level to be available to receive grievances on at least one designated day every week. This requirement has been removed, making it harder for workers to know when and where they can approach officials. 5.⁠ ⁠Removal of dedicated grievance redressal desks: The draft mandated grievance redressal desks at every Block and District to facilitate registration of complaints and provide information about the implementation of the Act. This provision has been deleted. 6.⁠ ⁠Dilution of the requirement for physical verification of complaints: The draft explicitly required enquiries through spot verification or inspection. The final Rules permit examination of official records and other information but do not expressly require physical verification. This is particularly problematic where complaints concern falsification of muster rolls, fraudulent payments or discrepancies between official records and ground realities. 7.⁠ ⁠Removal of mandatory quarterly reporting: The draft required the DPC to submit quarterly reports to the State Government detailing the number, nature and categories of grievances, along with their disposal and pendency. This provision has been deleted, weakening institutional monitoring and accountability. 8.⁠ ⁠Weakening of automatic escalation: The draft explicitly required grievances unresolved within fifteen days to be automatically escalated to the next higher authority through the digital platform. The final Rules retain mandatory escalation after fifteen days but remove the explicit requirement that it be automatic. 9.⁠ ⁠Removal of an explicitly mandated State-level grievance redressal mechanism: The draft required State Governments to establish grievance redressal mechanisms at Gram Panchayat, Block, District and State levels. The final Rules expressly specify only Gram Panchayat, Block and District levels, although they allow other levels to be designated. 10.⁠ ⁠Removal of detailed appellate provisions from the Rules: The draft explicitly specified the appellate hierarchy, a 45-day period for filing appeals and a 30-day deadline for their disposal. The final Rules replace these provisions with a reference to Schedule I of the Act. Whether this reduces the substantive right of appeal depends on the corresponding provisions of the parent Act. 11.⁠ ⁠Reduced flexibility for State-level digital grievance systems: The draft recognised digital grievance platforms provided by either the Central or State Government. The final Rules place greater emphasis on a Central Government-designated digital platform, reducing the express flexibility available to States. Without making sufficient financial allocations, ensuring the realisation of the guarantees is the sole burden of the State, and there is no avenue by which people can ensure redress for what are daily violations. Using the mirage of digital governance, the rules clearly demonstrate that the rights will remain on paper / in the cloud. Today while millions of workers are not able to record their attendance through (National Mobile Monitoring System) NMMS, are not able to receive their wages due to Aadhaar-Based Payment System (ABPS), even grievances are now going to be placed in the digital domain without accountability.

According to the Congress leader, one of the most significant changes was deleting a draft provision that treated failure to dispose of grievances within seven working days as a contravention of the Act, potentially inviting action under Section 27. While timelines have been retained, the final rules do not explicitly prescribe accountability for officials who fail to meet them, he said.

Mr. Ramesh further criticised the deletion of provisions mandating review of grievance-related action by Intermediate and District Panchayats, establishment of dedicated grievance redressal desks at block and district levels, and designation of a fixed weekly day for officials to receive complaints.

The Congress leader said the final rules had also weakened provisions relating to physical verification of complaints, quarterly reporting by district authorities, automatic escalation of unresolved grievances, and State-level grievance redressal mechanisms. He argued that the changes reduced transparency and democratic oversight.

Mr. Ramesh contended that the increasing reliance on digital platforms for grievance filing could further disadvantage rural workers already facing difficulties linked to the National Mobile Monitoring System and the Aadhaar-Based Payment System.

“Using the mirage of digital governance, the rules clearly demonstrate that the rights will remain on paper and in the cloud,” he said, adding that millions of workers continued to face challenges in recording attendance and receiving wages.

articles.title: 24 hours after High Court rap, BMC fails to restore Dia Mirza’s video on pollution-free Diwali
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: Civil rights activist Sumaira Abdulali, who has been working for the cause of noise pollution, demanded that the BMC should give an explanation about why it had pulled down a video which was recorded as per the directives of the Bombay High Court

Over 24 hours after the Bombay High Court directed the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC) to restore the video message of actor Dia Mirza’s appeal for a noise-free and pollution-free Diwali, the BMC has failed to do so. Sources in the BMC say they will study the court order and take an appropriate call on it. They refused to give a timeline for the restoration of the video. Meanwhile, the opposition and civil rights organisations hit out at the government for the lapse. Shiv Sena UBT demanded that the civic body should restore the video immediately.

“The BJP regime is now blatantly disrespecting the Honourable Court. Firstly, it criticised Dia’s video because of her surname. The video was made for an appeal of the High Court order itself. Then the BJP calls her anti-national. For what? Raising environmental issues? Making a video appeal for a court order? The regime can’t handle the administration – be it the city or the country,” Shiv Sena UBT leader Aditya Thackeray told T he Hindu on Wednesday (November 4, 2026).

Civil rights activist Sumaira Abdulali, who has been working for the cause of noise pollution, demanded that the BMC should give an explanation about why it had pulled down a video which was recorded as per the directives of the Bombay High Court.

“The reason they took it down was not explainable. They were only following the court order. How can a politician interfere in a court order? The second question is to ignore the order 24 hours later. The government is not respecting the court of law. The noise rules were made in the year 2000. The first orders started coming around in the year 2003. We have still not been following those court orders. The intention seems to be not to follow the court order in this aspect (noise pollution). Whether we are going to follow them or not is the real question. The record shows that we don’t,” she told The Hindu .

She said that she was similarly targeted for raising voice against noise pollution. “Instead of following the court order, we are tarnishing people for other reasons, which is subverting the law. This is very brazen. But it has been happening for a long time. I have been targeted for years in the same way,” she said.

Last week, the BMC had uploaded the videos of celebrities appealing to people to celebrate noise-free and air pollution-free Diwali. This was done as per the directions of the Bombay High Court. The celebrities who participated in the voluntary campaign included Madhuri Dixit, cricketer Ajinkya Rahane, actor Nishigandha Wad and UN Goodwill ambassador Dia Mirza.

Soon thereafter, BJP Mumbai president Ameet Satam had publicly posted against Ms. Mirza, telling the BMC that they do not need her advice to celebrate their festival. This had led to the BMC pulling down the tweet. The Bombay High Court took note of this and expressed displeasure at the move. It directed the BMC to restore the video message of Ms. Mirza. The orders were issued on October 3 (Tuesday).

BMC sources said that the law and judiciary department officials were busy on Wednesday (November 4) with the urgent demolition drive, which was held in Borivali. That drive was held after the Supreme Court had ordered the withholding of BMC Commissioner’s salary for the failure to raze illegal structures. “We will study the order and take a decision on it,” a BMC official said.

In the order issued on November 3, the Bombay High Court has also asked the Maharashtra government if it can designate regulated timings for the bursting of firecrackers during Diwali to prevent health hazards and environmental damage.

articles.title: Centre earmarks ₹2,814 crore to boost lithium, nickel processing
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: In a social media post, Union Coal and Mines Minister G. Kishan Reddy stated the scheme would help strengthen domestic capabilities, boost manufacturing and reduce dependence on imports.

The Union Cabinet on Wednesday approved a ₹2,814-crore capital expenditure support scheme to establish domestic processing facilities for lithium and nickel, seeking to strengthen India’s critical mineral ecosystem and reduce import dependence. The scheme will remain in force for five years.

India’s domestic beneficiation and processing infrastructure for critical minerals remains limited, with commercial-scale operations constrained by high capital requirements, limited access to suitable technologies and inadequate availability of raw materials, the government said in a statement.
Union Minister for Coal and Mines G. Kishan Reddy said the scheme would strengthen domestic capabilities, boost manufacturing and reduce dependence on imports.

“It will benefit key sectors such as electronics, semiconductors, batteries, defence, heavy equipment and machinery, while supporting industries across the manufacturing value chain that utilise critical minerals,” he said in a social media post.
Under the scheme, the government will provide a capital subsidy of 30% of the investment required to establish four critical mineral processing plants — two each for lithium and nickel.
The minimum processing capacity will be 30,000 tonnes (30 kt) each for lithium and 50,000 tonnes (50 kt) each for nickel.
The subsidy will be capped at ₹500 crore per beneficiary for lithium projects and ₹900 crore per beneficiary for nickel facilities.

The four beneficiaries will be selected through a least-cost bidding process, with preference given to technically qualified applicants seeking the lowest capital expenditure support. Incentives will be disbursed in three tranches.

Industry body the Federation of Indian Mineral Industries (FIMI) welcomed the initiative, saying it could encourage fresh investments, increase domestic value addition and strengthen supply chains for battery manufacturing and other strategic industries.
However, it said that securing adequate raw materials would be critical to the scheme’s success.

articles.title: Union Cabinet approves new VISTAR scheme to overhaul India’s statistical system
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: The three-pronged scheme is aimed at strengthening data collecting, analysis, the incorporation of AI, as well as provide fresh data on the unorganised sector to make the overall GDP figure more accurate

The Union Cabinet on Wednesday approved a ₹4,371 crore scheme to overhaul the statistical architecture of the country at both the Central as well as State level, called the Viksit Bharat Initiative for Statistical Transformation, Analytics & Research (VISTAR) scheme, for the period 2026-27 to 2030-31.

“Aligned with the central objective of Viksit Bharat 2047, the VISTAR Scheme is designed to establish a dynamic, real-time and future-ready official statistical architecture for enhanced timeliness, data granularity, interoperability with harmonised and AI ready datasets,” the government said in a release.

As per the government, the VISTAR scheme will be divided into three components: Comprehensive statistical operations and strengthening of the ecosystem, Support for statistical strengthening, and an Economic Census.

Under the Comprehensive Statistical Operations and Strengthening of Ecosystem component, the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) has proposed to conduct 59 surveys during the 16th Finance Commission cycle, as compared to 43 major surveys conducted previously.
This, the government said, could potentially fill “critical data gaps in various sectors” and thereby improve decision-making and enable timely and targeted policy interventions.

“In addition, building on recent digital transformations in technology enabled data collection and user-centric dissemination, MoSPI will focus on the end-to-end digitalisation of statistical processes and embedding Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning into regular workflows, primarily for data processing, validation, and analysis,” the government added.

The three-pronged scheme is aimed at strengthening data collecting, analysis, the incorporation of AI, as well as provide fresh data on the unorganised sector to make the overall GDP figure more accurate

The Union Cabinet on Wednesday approved a ₹4,371 crore scheme to overhaul the statistical architecture of the country at both the Central as well as State level, called the Viksit Bharat Initiative for Statistical Transformation, Analytics & Research (VISTAR) scheme, for the period 2026-27 to 2030-31.

“Aligned with the central objective of Viksit Bharat 2047, the VISTAR Scheme is designed to establish a dynamic, real-time and future-ready official statistical architecture for enhanced timeliness, data granularity, interoperability with harmonised and AI ready datasets,” the government said in a release.

As per the government, the VISTAR scheme will be divided into three components: Comprehensive statistical operations and strengthening of the ecosystem, Support for statistical strengthening, and an Economic Census.

Under the Comprehensive Statistical Operations and Strengthening of Ecosystem component, the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) has proposed to conduct 59 surveys during the 16th Finance Commission cycle, as compared to 43 major surveys conducted previously.

This, the government said, could potentially fill “critical data gaps in various sectors” and thereby improve decision-making and enable timely and targeted policy interventions.

“In addition, building on recent digital transformations in technology enabled data collection and user-centric dissemination, MoSPI will focus on the end-to-end digitalisation of statistical processes and embedding Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning into regular workflows, primarily for data processing, validation, and analysis,” the government added.

Further, it added that, by mainstreaming alternate sources such as mobile phones, scanners, and e-commerce data, MoSPI will aim to complement traditional surveys, reduce respondent burden, fill data gaps, and strengthen evidence-based policymaking.

Under the support for statistical strengthening (SSS) component, the Centre will provide funds to State governments to help transform the statistical capabilities of States and Union Territories through a redesigned, deliverable-linked framework.

“The vision focuses on building state-level capacity to generate high-quality, granular data at the district and other disaggregated levels, developing indigenous data processing capabilities, and embedding data use cases into localized policymaking,” the government said.

MoSPI will also undertake the 8th Economic Census (EC) in collaboration with the States and Union Territories in order to obtain granular data and activity details of all the non-farm establishments and workers hired down to the gram panchayat and ward levels

articles.title: Union Cabinet approves ₹14,500 crore VGF scheme to develop large scale energy storage in India
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: The scheme is designed to provide for the development of hydro pumped storage plant (PSP) capacity, battery energy storage system (BESS) capacity, as well as alternative energy storage technologies

The Union Cabinet has approved a ₹14,500 crore Viability Gap Funding (VGF) scheme for the development of grid-scale energy storage systems for the period 2026-27 to 2030-31, the government announced on Wednesday.
According to the government, the scheme is aimed at supporting the development of 92 GWh of fresh, yet-to-be-commissioned, energy storage capacity across the country.

“The scheme will support creation of new capacities equivalent to 170% of the present-day grid scale energy storage system capacity in the country and help meet the required grid scale ESS capacity of 411 GWh by 2031-32,” the government said in a release.
ALSO WATCH Watch: Can battery storage save India’s renewable energy grid? | Business Matters

The scheme is designed to provide for the development of 60 GWh of hydro pumped storage plant (PSP) capacity, 30 GWh of battery energy storage system (BESS) capacity and 2 GWh of capacity through alternative energy storage technologies, with a total estimated investment of ₹97,600 crore.

“The VGF support will help improve the financial viability of these projects and accelerate the deployment of large-scale energy storage infrastructure in the country,” the government said, adding that the scheme will also provide an impetus to domestic manufacturing of battery energy storage systems.

As per the government’s release, energy storage capacity will be allocated through a tariff-based competitive bidding process with both public and private sector electricity distribution companies eligible for VGF support for BESS and hydro PSP projects.
Projects based on alternative energy storage technologies, too, will be implemented by public and private sector entities.

“To promote indigenous manufacturing, BESS projects will be subject to a minimum Domestic Content Requirement (DCR) of 40%,” the government added. “The requirement will encourage domestic manufacturing, create opportunities for Indian industry and complement existing supply-side incentives for battery manufacturing.”

articles.title: U.S. midterm elections impact on India: Faster trade deal talks and higher tariffs likely
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: Trade and geopolitical experts say that losing control of the U.S. Congress will push President Donald Trump to increase tariff pressure on India to seal a deal. Indian negotiators, for their part, will smell an opportunity

The results of the U.S. midterm elections, which show that the Democrats have gained control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives, will likely speed up talks between India and the U.S. on a trade deal but could also see higher tariffs on India until the deal is closed, according to experts.

On the one hand, a desire to now quickly close the trade deal to show strength domestically could induce Mr. Trump to increase his tariff pressure on India, while on the other, Indian negotiators will likely see this election result as an opportunity to push through a favourable deal for India.
U.S. midterm elections: Follow LIVE updates from the results on November 4, 2026

According to Ajay Srivastava, founder of the trade think-tank Global Trade Research Initiative, this loss will push U.S. President Donald Trump to increase his exercise of his executive powers to pressure India into accepting a deal.
“With foreign policy leverage failing against Russia, China, and Iran, Trump needs a quick win,” Mr. Srivastava said. “Expect heightened pressure on India for a trade deal to prove American clout.”

Leaders in the U.S. and India have repeatedly said over the last few months that the deal between the two countries is nearly ready and is awaiting final approvals. India, in particular, has been holding out until it receives an assurance that it will win a clear advantage over its competitors.

“Trump will now use his executive powers to pressure India for a quick deal that secures market access for U.S. agricultural and industrial goods, alongside other major concessions for U.S. companies,” Mr. Srivastava said.

While the U.S. Supreme Court in February defanged Mr. Trump’s reciprocal tariff policy that had seen tariffs of up to 50% being levied on India, the President has other tools through which he can levy tariffs.

According to Deep Pal, Director of Geopolitics and Policy at the Koan Advisory Group, the implications of these election results might lead to some difficulty for Mr. Trump in gaining support for his policies.

“For this administration, especially after tonight, any decision has to look like a win domestically, to core Republican voters,” Mr. Pal said. “With Congress out of his hands, a lot will depend on how much control Mr. Trump has over the Republican party and if there will be any purchase for his ideas.”

The results of the U.S. midterm elections, which show that the Democrats have gained control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives, will likely speed up talks between India and the U.S. on a trade deal but could also see higher tariffs on India until the deal is closed, according to experts.

articles.title: Supreme Court upholds States’ power to levy additional sales tax, says case has become academic
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: The seven-judge Bench, led by CJI Surya Kant, said the reference in the Orissa Sales Tax Act case no longer requires adjudication since the challenged provisions have been amended and GST governs the issue moving forward

The Supreme Court on Wednesday (November 4, 2026) held that a 1974 Constitution Bench ruling upholding States’ power to impose additional sales tax or surcharge calculated as a percentage of the existing sales tax continues to hold the field, saying a reference on the issue had become academic.

A seven-judge Constitution Bench headed by Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant unanimously held that the legal question referred to it nearly 27 years ago no longer required adjudication, as the statutory provisions under challenge had since been replaced or amended and the Goods and Services Tax (GST) law had come into force.

“The question referred to is of no practical significance and now academic. Consequently, the question referred to does not survive for adjudication by a seven-judge Bench, and the reference has to be answered accordingly,” the CJI, who wrote the judgment on behalf of himself and five other judges, said.
The Bench also comprised Justices K.V. Viswanathan, S.V.N. Bhatti, Joymalya Bagchi, N.V. Anjaria, Arun Palli and V. Mohana.
Justice Viswanathan wrote a separate concurring verdict.

While declining to undertake a fresh adjudication on the reference, the Court clarified that the five-judge Constitution Bench ruling in S. Kodar vs State of Kerala (1974) continued to hold the field.
The earlier judgment had upheld additional sales tax, rejecting the argument that such a levy amounted to a tax on the income of dealers.

“We have clarified that the case clearly held that an additional tax or surcharge computed as a percentage of the sales tax payable is an enhancement of the rate of sales tax and a tax on the sale or purchase of goods within Entry 54 of List II, as it then stood. That decision continues to hold the field,” the CJI said.
The Court further held that the question of the legislative competence of State legislatures to impose the surcharge would be governed by the law laid down in S. Kodar.

The reference arose from a challenge to Section 5A of the Orissa Sales Tax Act, 1947, which provided for additional tax at the rate of 10% on dealers with an annual turnover between ₹10 lakh and ₹1 crore, and 15% on dealers whose turnover exceeded ₹1 crore.

articles.title: Services sector activity hits 4-month high in October as business conditions improve cautiously
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: Survey participants identified new business growth as the main driver behind the rise in output, the survey said

India's services sector activity recorded the strongest pace of expansion in four months in October as demand buoyancy fuelled growth in business activity and new orders amid easing cost pressures, a monthly survey said on Wednesday (November 4, 2026).
Companies were cautiously optimistic about the outlook, and they lifted jobs to the least extent in four months. The latest expansion in international sales was the weakest in almost four years.
The seasonally adjusted HSBC India Services PMI Business Activity Index rose from 55.2 in September to 55.8 in October, indicating the strongest pace of growth for four months.
In the Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) parlance, a print above 50 means expansion, while a score below 50 denotes contraction.

"India's services PMI rose to 55.8 in October, a four-month high, as business conditions improved cautiously. Although overall demand remained fairly strong, new export orders recorded the slowest pace of expansion since February 2023," Pranjul Bhandari, Chief India Economist at HSBC, said.

Survey participants identified new business growth as the main driver behind the rise in output, the survey said, adding that favourable demand conditions, new client wins and successful advertising boosted new order intakes.

On the prices front, there was a substantial decline in cost pressures. "Input and output prices continued to rise, but at a slower pace than in the previous month, signalling some relief from inflation pressures," Bhandari said.
Employment growth also slowed to its weakest pace since June, suggesting that some service sector businesses have sufficient capacity to meet current staffing requirements, she said.
Companies were, however, cautiously optimistic about the outlook, and they lifted jobs to the least extent in four months.
Meanwhile, India's composite PMI increased to 56.2 in October, from 55.9 in September, marking the fastest rise in aggregate output in four months and reflecting healthy business activity.

articles.title: U.S. judge temporarily blocks deportation of detained Afghans to Afghanistan or Pakistan
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: The order pauses planned removals until Saturday after advocates and lawmakers warned that deported Afghans could face persecution, torture or death

A federal judge in New York temporarily blocked the Trump administration’s plans to deport Afghans detained in the United States to Afghanistan or Pakistan on Tuesday (November 3, 2026), after advocates and dozens of members of Congress warned that their lives would be at risk.

The government told the court on Tuesday (November 3, 2026) that Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) had no chartered or commercial flights to deport Afghan nationals to Afghanistan or Pakistan at least until the end of the week. Judge Valerie Caproni’s order, which expires on Saturday (November 7, 2026), directs officials to adhere to that statement. ICE books deportation flights weeks in advance.

A letter led by California Democratic Representative Scott Peters and signed by 65 other members of the House and Senate said they were “extremely concerned that sending vulnerable people” would expose them to “persecution, torture, or even death”. The letter was sent on Monday (November 2, 2026) to Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin.
Immigrant rights organisations have also warned that those deported could face retaliation from the Taliban.
Thousands of Afghans fled persecution and feared for their lives after helping the U.S. military and aid groups in Afghanistan.

According to court documents obtained by the Associated Press, the U.S. planned to deport Afghan immigrants on Monday on flights from Louisiana, where ICE has detention and processing facilities, to Pakistan.

President Donald Trump’s administration has deported thousands of immigrants to countries other than their own. In some cases, it has used third-country deportations when removal to a person’s country of origin was not possible, including when formal diplomatic relations were absent, as is the case with Afghanistan’s Taliban government. In other instances, third-country deportations have been used as a deterrent.

Advocates and attorneys said more than 80 detained Afghans had contacted them after ICE notified them that they could be deported this week via Pakistan. They include women, a police officer, members of religious minorities and people whose family members served in the U.S. military. Most fled Afghanistan because of persecution and do not have legal representation, according to Human Rights First and AfghanEvac, a nonprofit organisation that advocates for immigrants.

Before the judge signed her order, Zia Ahmad Takal, deputy spokesman for Afghanistan’s foreign ministry, said “the Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan expresses its serious concern” about reports that the U.S. planned to transfer Afghans to Pakistan.

Mr. Takal called on the U.S. to ensure that decisions or actions were based on the rights and “legitimate demands” of those involved. He said “third-party countries should not engage in dealings concerning the fate of another nation’s citizens”.

articles.title: Bangladesh agrees new garment pay scale from December amid protests
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: Workers are demanding the monthly minimum wage be raised to 30,000 taka ($242) from 12,500 taka, saying rising food, housing and transport costs have eroded their purchasing power

Bangladesh's newly formed wage board agreed on ‌Wednesday (November 4, 2026) to implement a revised pay structure for garment workers from December, ​as protests over wages entered their fifth day and disrupted production in ⁠the country's key apparel sector.

The board did not discuss the size of any wage increase and will hold further meetings to determine the new pay structure, Babul Akter, the workers' representative on the ‌board, said after its first meeting.
"The new wage structure will be implemented from December, and workers will receive their first salaries under the revised pay scale ‌in January," Mr. Akter said.

The six-member board was formed this week amid growing labour unrest ‌and ⁠includes representatives of workers and factory owners. It is responsible for reviewing ⁠pay in Bangladesh's garment industry.
Workers are demanding the monthly minimum wage be raised to 30,000 taka ($242) from 12,500 taka, saying rising food, housing and transport costs have eroded their purchasing power.

Clashes broke out on ​Wednesday (November 4, 2026) between workers and police in Savar ‌and Gazipur, two major garment manufacturing hubs on the outskirts of Dhaka. Protesters blocked roads and highways, while police used tear gas and sound grenades. Several factories suspended operations amid fears of further unrest.

Hundreds of garment factories have shut this week during ‌a crucial production period for spring and summer export orders, raising concerns about shipment ​delays in Bangladesh, the world's second-largest garment exporter after China.
The sector employs about 4 million workers, generates more than 80% of Bangladesh's export earnings ⁠, and supplies brands including H&M, Inditex's Zara and Walmart.
"Every month is a struggle," said Bithi Begum, a garment worker. "After working hard all day, the money we earn is hardly enough to ‌cover even our basic needs."
International retailers are closely monitoring the situation as factories enter a key production period for spring and summer orders.

Workers are demanding the monthly minimum wage be raised to 30,000 taka ($242) from 12,500 taka, saying rising food, housing and transport costs have eroded their purchasing power

Bangladesh's newly formed wage board agreed on ‌Wednesday (November 4, 2026) to implement a revised pay structure for garment workers from December, ​as protests over wages entered their fifth day and disrupted production in ⁠the country's key apparel sector.

The board did not discuss the size of any wage increase and will hold further meetings to determine the new pay structure, Babul Akter, the workers' representative on the ‌board, said after its first meeting.

"The new wage structure will be implemented from December, and workers will receive their first salaries under the revised pay scale ‌in January," Mr. Akter said.

The six-member board was formed this week amid growing labour unrest ‌and ⁠includes representatives of workers and factory owners. It is responsible for reviewing ⁠pay in Bangladesh's garment industry.

Workers are demanding the monthly minimum wage be raised to 30,000 taka ($242) from 12,500 taka, saying rising food, housing and transport costs have eroded their purchasing power.

Clashes broke out on ​Wednesday (November 4, 2026) between workers and police in Savar ‌and Gazipur, two major garment manufacturing hubs on the outskirts of Dhaka. Protesters blocked roads and highways, while police used tear gas and sound grenades. Several factories suspended operations amid fears of further unrest.

Hundreds of garment factories have shut this week during ‌a crucial production period for spring and summer export orders, raising concerns about shipment ​delays in Bangladesh, the world's second-largest garment exporter after China.

The sector employs about 4 million workers, generates more than 80% of Bangladesh's export earnings ⁠, and supplies brands including H&M, Inditex's Zara and Walmart.

"Every month is a struggle," said Bithi Begum, a garment worker. "After working hard all day, the money we earn is hardly enough to ‌cover even our basic needs."

articles.title: United Nations report says genocide continues in Gaza
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: The Israeli violations include widespread or systematic attacks directed against the civilian population, state policy, and the fact that the security forces knew the acts constituted part of an attack against the civilian population and so intended them (mens rea)

The Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including East Jerusalem, and Israel has concluded that Israeli authorities and forces have continued to commit war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide in the occupied Palestinian territory even after the ceasefire agreement in Gaza.

In its report, submitted to the United Nations General Assembly on October 14, 2026, the Commission examines killings and serious bodily and mental harm inflicted by Israeli and Palestinian security forces since October 2023.

The commission sets out its findings regarding the drivers of Israeli and Palestinian state violence, in particular killings and bodily and mental harm, including sexual and gender-based violence. As part of a broader investigation into the root causes of recurrent tensions, instability, and protraction of the conflict, this report also reviews policies and practices examining drivers of violence.
As part of its mandate to look into underlying root causes, the Commission also asked for information relating to incidents from the periods 1948-1949, the 1950s, and the years 2000-2005.

The analysis was against the backdrop of the United Nations General Assembly Resolution 181 from 1947, which terminated the British Mandate on Palestine and adopted the partition plan, dividing the territory into three parts: two states, one Arab and one Jewish, and Jerusalem under International Control.

The report noted that the perception of Palestinians and a possible Palestinian state as “a threat to Israel and the desire to reduce Palestinian population” contributed to a permissive military culture where Israeli soldiers, with or without directives from commanders, directly target Palestinians whether or not they pose a real or immediate threat.

According to the report, from October 7, 2023 to October 9, 2025, more than 72,600 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza and more than 1,000 in the West Bank. From October 10, 2025 to September 30, 2026, 1,431 Palestinians were killed in Gaza and 137 in the West Bank.

The commission has made findings in its previous reports on the actions of Israeli forces in Gaza amounting to genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes, in addition to violations of international humanitarian and human rights law.

It also found that the killing and harming of children and sexual- and gender-based violence are included among elements that established specific intent of the Israeli authorities to commit genocide against the Palestinian group in Gaza.

The Commission had previously reported on the Israeli forces’ use of artificial intelligence tools and autonomous weapons systems in Gaza, expressing its concerns about these weapons’ compliance with International law.

articles.title: Ukraine's Zelenskyy awards U.S. first lady Melania state honour
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: The award — the Order ‌of Princess Olga, ​1st class — honours women who have made exceptional ⁠contributions in spheres including science, education, culture and charitable ‌work

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has awarded the U.S. ​first lady Melania Trump ‌a state honour for her ​role in helping ⁠to organise a humanitarian evacuation from a frontline town last ‌week, according to a decree published on Wednesday (November 4, 2026).

The ‌Presidential decree, dated ‌November ⁠2, cited her "significant ⁠personal contribution" to humanitarian support for Ukraine and her work to ​help Ukrainian ‌children, including those deported or forcibly moved from Russian-occupied territory.
The award — the Order ‌of Princess Olga, ​1st class — honours women who have made exceptional ⁠contributions in spheres including science, education, culture and charitable ‌work.

Ukrainian officials have said Melania Trump played a pivotal role in organising the six-day ceasefire to evacuate civilians from the ‌Russian-occupied southern Ukrainian town of ​Oleshky, which concluded on Sunday (November 1, 2026).
It was the longest ⁠local pause in fighting since ⁠Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022. Nearly 800 ‌people were evacuated, Ms. Trump said.

articles.title: NVS-03 reaches geosynchronous orbit; satellite in good health
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: ‘Four orbit manoeuvres have been successfully completed with a cumulative LAM engine burn of 6164 seconds; with this the satellite has reached Geo Synchronous Orbit at an inclination of 29.980,’ said ISRO
The NVS-03 satellite launched by the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) on October 30, 2026, has reached the intended Geo Synchronous Orbit.

ISRO said in an update on Wednesday (November 4, 2026) that following four successful orbit manoeuvres, the satellite has reached Geo Synchronous Orbit (35765 km x 36196 km) at an inclination of 29.980.

“Four orbit manoeuvres have been successfully completed with a cumulative LAM engine burn of 6164 seconds. With this the satellite has reached Geo Synchronous Orbit [35765 km x 36196 km] at an inclination of 29.980,” ISRO said.
The NVS-03 satellite was successfully injected into 170.3 km x 38080 km orbit by GSLV on October 30.
The NVS-03 is the third satellite in the next generation navigation satellite system envisaged for providing continuity of navigation services for the IRNSS series.

The satellite carries indigenous atomic clock along with the procured clocks. It also includes L1 signal in addition to L5 and S band signals with coverage over Indian land mass and a region extending 1500 km around Indian geopolitical boundary.
The space agency also said that the satellite’s health is normal.

The development is significant as ISRO in 2025 was unable to perform the intended orbit raising operations for the NVS-02 satellite due to a valve malfunction. The NVS-02, the second satellite in the NVS series, was launched by the ISRO on January 29, 2025.

articles.title: Apollo Foundation’s hospital in Aragonda blends healthcare with education, nutrition and sanitation
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: What if improving the health of a village meant doing more than building a hospital, treating patients and performing surgeries? In Aragonda, a village in Andhra Pradesh’s Chittoor district, an initiative that began with a 50-bed rural hospital has evolved into a community development model that links healthcare with education, nutrition, sanitation and preventive health.

Through its Total Health programme, Apollo Foundation is attempting to address the wider social determinants of health, with interventions spanning different stages of people’s lives, from maternal and child healthcare to youth development, women’s economic independence and elderly care.

The programme’s interventions include 1,200 antenatal and postnatal check-ups for new mothers, training in hygiene practices across 2,600 schools and industry-related and sports skills for more than 545 young people. It has also conducted over two lakh yoga sessions, alongside free screening and care for non-communicable diseases (NCDs), while more than 10.8 lakh meals have been served to elderly people through its geriatric nutrition centres.

Prathap C. Reddy, founder chairman of Apollo Hospitals Group, said the initiative reflected his belief that quality and affordable healthcare should reach every Indian, irrespective of where they lived. While the hospital initially brought modern medicine to his village, the larger vision was to create conditions in which people could lead healthier lives, he said. “Medicine can save lives, but to change the health of a generation, we must also change the conditions in which life is lived,” he added.

Alongside preventive and community healthcare, Apollo Hospitals Aragonda has also expanded its specialised surgical services, completing 1,000 total knee replacement (TKR) procedures. Established as a 50-bed hospital in 2000, it has served more than 1.67 lakh patients and performed over 12,000 surgeries in 26 years.

The knee replacement programme has grown from 100 procedures in 2019 to 500 in 2022 and 1,000 in 2026. “The 1,000 procedures have been completed without a single reported infection,” said Sangita Reddy, joint managing director of Apollo Hospitals.

Telemedicine was another early intervention. With a network of three telephone lines, Apollo connected specialists in cities with patients in rural areas, allowing doctors to examine CT scans and ultrasound images remotely. The initiative enabled specialists to guide local doctors in treating patients who otherwise would have had to travel to distant hospitals. She recalled that former President of US, Bill Clinton, witnessed a telemedicine demonstration from Aragonda during his visit to Hyderabad.

Preetha Reddy, executive vice-chairperson of Apollo Hospitals Enterprise Limited said the organisation remained committed to narrowing the divide between rural and urban healthcare. “The ability to perform specialised procedures such as knee replacements in a village demonstrates the potential for such models to be replicated in other parts of the world,” she added.

articles.title: Why even a strong El Niño does not guarantee a poor Indian monsoon
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: Seven Indian monsoons since 1950 have run into a moderate or strong El Niño. Of these, in five years, including 2026, monsoon rainfall levels were at least 10% lower than the long-term average. The IMD refers to this level as 'deficient’. The 2023 season was something of an exception with ‘below average’ rainfall. However, 1997 had ‘average’ rainfall

In the summer of 1997, one of the strongest El Niños of the 20th century took shape in the Pacific Ocean. The India Meteorological Department (IMD) predicted a monsoon rainfall deficit of 8% below the average, as was expected in El Niño years. However, by the end of September that year, rainfall levels were nearly normal.

This year, a “ferocious” El Niño is taking shape, and is expected to peak only in December. The 2026 southwest monsoon ended nearly 13% below the long-term average of 87 cm. East and Northeast India had their driest season since records began in 1901.

articles.title: Russian attacks disrupt power in Kyiv, while death toll in a stricken village rises to 40
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: Russia attacked overnight with 310 drones, including 81 jet-powered drones, according to Ukraine’s air force. In its daily social media report, the air force said it downed or suppressed 272 drones of various types

Russian attacks triggered power and water outages for hours on Wednesday (November 4, 2026) across Kyiv and surrounding regions, while President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the death toll in a stricken village in southern Ukraine rose to 40 in one of the deadliest strikes there in nearly five years of war.

On Monday (November 2, 2026), multiple Russian guided bombs slammed into a former school and a nearby shelter in the village of Komyshuvakha, near the front line in the Zaporizhzhia region, as residents waited for humanitarian aid.
In addition to those killed, Mr. Zelenskyy said 30 more people could still be buried in the rubble.

“Unfortunately, there has been very little reaction from the world to this insane attack," he said in a post on X. "But it, like thousands upon thousands of other war crimes Russia has committed against Ukraine and Ukrainians, demands a strong response. Evil always goes further if it is left unanswered.”
Elsewhere, Moscow showed no signs of letting up its aerial assaults.

Before water and power were restored, residents in the capital of Kyiv were urged to use public drinking water fountains. Emergency centres were set up hastily in the worst-hit areas, offering hot tea and power for people seeking to charge electrical devices.

Russia attacked overnight with 310 drones, including 81 jet-powered drones, according to Ukraine’s air force. In its daily social media report, the air force said it downed or suppressed 272 drones of various types.

Such attacks are a regular feature of wartime life in Ukraine, despite arrest warrants issued by the International Criminal Court in 2024 for two senior Russian officers whom prosecutors accuse of overseeing strikes on civilian infrastructure.

Officials from the United States, Germany, France, Britain, NATO, and the European Union were to meet later on Wednesday (November 4, 2026) at the European Commission’s headquarters in Brussels. The discussions are expected to focus on security arrangements for postwar Ukraine, the massive reconstruction effort that will be required, and also various “economic opportunities” that peace could bring.

EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the meeting, expected to stretch into Thursday (November 5, 2026), to discuss European demands for Russian concessions in any negotiations. She said previous talks have focused only on “what Ukraine should give away or what concessions they should make.”

articles.title: South Africa votes as ANC faces further losses and coalition rule looms
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: The ANC’s support could fall below 40%, while the Democratic Alliance is projected to gain ground in Johannesburg

South Africans voted in municipal elections on Wednesday (November 4, 2026), with anger over corruption, crime and failing public services threatening to deal another blow to the African National Congress (ANC).
The party of Nelson Mandela fell below 50% support for the first time in the 2021 municipal elections and could drop below 40% this time, according to polls.

With no other party large enough to replace it, many cities are heading towards unstable coalition governments. Such arrangements have been partly blamed for failures to deliver basic services, including water and electricity.

The election outcome will set the stage for the next national election in 2029 and could influence the ANC’s succession race as President Cyril Ramaphosa approaches the end of his term as party leader in 2027.

“Municipal failures have contributed to declining public trust and confidence in democratic governance,” Mr. Ramaphosa said. He has acknowledged failures within his party but expressed optimism that it would regain support.

Control of Johannesburg, South Africa’s commercial hub, is the biggest prize. The race remained open after an energetic mayoral campaign by Democratic Alliance (DA) candidate Helen Zille, who was projected to win the most votes but fall short of a majority.

Other metro areas to watch include Tshwane, home to the administrative capital Pretoria, and eThekwini, which includes the port city of Durban and where former president Jacob Zuma’s uMkhonto weSizwe party is strong.
The DA is heavily favoured to retain control of Cape Town.
Local governance has been a weak point for the ANC, which was forced into a coalition with the DA and smaller parties after losing its national majority in 2024.

Although the ANC retains the loyalty of some voters because of its role in ending apartheid, growing numbers of South Africans are frustrated by power cuts and water shortages, including in Johannesburg. High unemployment and poor public safety are also major concerns.

The gathering of hundreds of thousands of people at Delhi’s Ramlila Maidan, organised by the Congress-led INDIA bloc parties, was a milestone in the battle for the restoration of the integrity of India’s election process. As more and more skeletons tumble out the of the closet of the Election Commission of India (ECI), its chief Gyanesh Kumar has chosen silence while the ruling BJP has rushed to shield him from criticism. The united outcry of protest by the Opposition, led by the Leader of Opposition Rahul Gandhi , is a strong signal of public opinion for the ruling party and India’s institutions, including the ECI, that appear complicit in a scheme that threatens the foundations of Indian democracy. What remains unexplained by the ECI and Mr. Kumar are malpractices in the Special Intensive Revision that could have the effect of subverting the popular will. Protestors on Sunday had arrived from all parts of India, and included people directly affected by the SIR across the country.

The protest reinforced Mr. Gandhi’s central role as the key challenger of Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Mr. Gandhi, for all his faults, has been an uncompromising champion of constitutional values and pluralism in India. The BJP caricatured him, and even non-BJP voices had bought into the idea of Mr. Gandhi being a privileged dynast out of touch with the commoner. While his ancestry is a matter of fact, so is his tenacity. All Opposition parties mobilised for the protest, but the centrality of the Congress party was unmistakable. Mr. Gandhi has a special focus on subaltern classes to be included in positions of responsibility in the party. The Sunday protest was clearly the largest show of strength in recent memory. The manner in which the Congress coordinated with the wide spectrum of the Opposition, often involving rivals in States, also indicates a clear sense of purpose and pragmatism. The call for the restoration of institutional integrity is the need of the hour; but Mr. Gandhi must be careful not to misstate the nature of the crisis. In his well-reasoned call for accountability of the ECI, Mr. Gandhi ended up questioning the legitimacy of the previous election without providing any substantive basis for his allegations. He must remember that his emergence as the voice of the Opposition places on him the responsibility of being measured in his speeches and his steps.

articles.title: Cascading effect: On dams and land rights
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: India must respect land rights of its people while building dams

The bureaucratic impetus for the 11.2-GW Siang Upper Multipurpose Project (SUMP) in Arunachal Pradesh purportedly comes from China’s aggressive development of a 60-GW mega-dam in Tibet , stoking anxieties among Indian authorities over ‘weaponised’ transboundary waters. Beijing may be able to divert flows in the Yarlung Tsangpo river, which becomes the Brahmaputra in India, to cause drought downstream or release water en masse to trigger catastrophic floods in Arunachal Pradesh and Assam. New Delhi thus imagines SUMP as a strategic buffer, but in so doing faces a dilemma it should not attempt to resolve with force. Its extant top-down approach, exemplified by deploying security forces to guard survey teams and imposing the State Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act against activists, only validates fears among locals that the state will grab their land. The region also hosts sustained protests against the Subansiri Upper Hydroelectric Project , expanding the indictment to Arunachal Pradesh’s model of hydroelectric power development. The eastern Himalayas are among the most tectonically active and erosion-prone landscapes in the world. The mega-dam in Tibet will comprise five cascading power stations over the river’s roughly 2,000-metre fall over 50 km. Beijing has maintained the dam will not harm countries downstream but has declined to share crucial engineering details. This is why diplomacy will be an essential part of operating SUMP, in addition to Beijing’s disputed claims on Arunachal Pradesh.

The Brahmaputra basin in Assam and Bangladesh receives most of its water from monsoon rains and tributaries downstream of the Tibetan Plateau, so China cannot straightforwardly control the river’s total flow through India. Yet since Chinese interventions would have greater consequences closer to the border, SUMP will need information about both the mega-dam’s operations and downstream inflows to plan its own operations, and Beijing has declined to share the former. SUMP thus faces many uncertainties at the outset. Despite India repeatedly raising the issue with China at the highest levels, headway has been limited to Beijing agreeing to share hydrological data on humanitarian grounds during emergencies. Planners have contemplated maintaining the SUMP reservoir at 70% to accommodate unexpected surges, but the level of protection possible if China supplies no advance warning remains unclear. This uncertainty is a thorn in the side of the government’s push against more legitimate resistance by Adi community members and civil rights groups. The need for the project does not excuse the state from following all the relevant laws and protections. The state cannot protect the nation’s needs by antagonising the nation’s people.

✍️ Editorial & Opinion 📅 03 Nov 2026 ⏱️ 3 Min Read

India must respect land rights of its people while building dams

The bureaucratic impetus for the 11.2-GW Siang Upper Multipurpose Project (SUMP) in Arunachal Pradesh purportedly comes from China’s aggressive development of a 60-GW mega-dam in Tibet , stoking anxieties among Indian authorities over ‘weaponised’ transboundary waters. Beijing may be able to divert flows in the Yarlung Tsangpo river, which becomes the Brahmaputra in India, to cause drought downstream or release water en masse to trigger catastrophic floods in Arunachal Pradesh and Assam. New Delhi thus imagines SUMP as a strategic buffer, but in so doing faces a dilemma it should not attempt to resolve with force. Its extant top-down approach, exemplified by deploying security forces to guard survey teams and imposing the State Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act against activists, only validates fears among locals that the state will grab their land. The region also hosts sustained protests against the Subansiri Upper Hydroelectric Project , expanding the indictment to Arunachal Pradesh’s model of hydroelectric power development. The eastern Himalayas are among the most tectonically active and erosion-prone landscapes in the world. The mega-dam in Tibet will comprise five cascading power stations over the river’s roughly 2,000-metre fall over 50 km. Beijing has maintained the dam will not harm countries downstream but has declined to share crucial engineering details. This is why diplomacy will be an essential part of operating SUMP, in addition to Beijing’s disputed claims on Arunachal Pradesh.

The Brahmaputra basin in Assam and Bangladesh receives most of its water from monsoon rains and tributaries downstream of the Tibetan Plateau, so China cannot straightforwardly control the river’s total flow through India. Yet since Chinese interventions would have greater consequences closer to the border, SUMP will need information about both the mega-dam’s operations and downstream inflows to plan its own operations, and Beijing has declined to share the former. SUMP thus faces many uncertainties at the outset. Despite India repeatedly raising the issue with China at the highest levels, headway has been limited to Beijing agreeing to share hydrological data on humanitarian grounds during emergencies. Planners have contemplated maintaining the SUMP reservoir at 70% to accommodate unexpected surges, but the level of protection possible if China supplies no advance warning remains unclear. This uncertainty is a thorn in the side of the government’s push against more legitimate resistance by Adi community members and civil rights groups. The need for the project does not excuse the state from following all the relevant laws and protections. The state cannot protect the nation’s needs by antagonising the nation’s people.

articles.title: Beyond gullibility: On digital arrest scams
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: Bank measures can only limit damage from ‘digital arrest’ scams

Chief Justice of India Surya Kant’s exasperation, during the Supreme Court’s hearing on October 29 on the “digital arrest” scams, that people still fall for such scams despite abundant warnings and orders from the Court is understandable. About ₹800 crore has been lost to these scams this year even after recoveries, a hefty sum from the savings of individual victims. But this is not merely about gullibility. Scammers posing as CBI or police officers succeed because their victims, older citizens in particular, defer to or fear law enforcement. When Indian police are widely seen as high-handed towards ordinary citizens and as serving only the powerful, the threat of an “arrest” over a video call cannot be that implausible for many. That said, the Court’s pressing of the Reserve Bank of India to finalise its KYC Amendment Directions, 2026, which require banks to flag suspected mule accounts and put temporary debit holds on them, is welcome. CBI investigations have shown that mule accounts are central to scammers laundering their proceeds after duping victims and that bank staff have, in some cases, helped open them. With the availability of complete transaction histories and AI tools, banks can now spot anomalous transactions faster. The Attorney-General’s assurance that the directions will be in force by December 31 is also welcome. The Court’s insistence that banks compensate victims addresses an issue with the RBI’s zero-liability provisions. Its 2017 circular covers only unauthorised transactions, leaving victims who were coerced into making transfers without any recourse.

Yet, full compensation for the victims whenever banks are found wanting in due diligence must be implemented with care as this might force banks to flag far more than the actual mule accounts. Already the RBI directions cast a wide net. Any transaction of ₹1,000 or more that is ‘unusual’ for an account holder’s declared profile, or linked to a reported account, can be held for up to 60 days, and longer if directed by the police. In cases where small traders and Jan Dhan account holders have unknowingly received transfers from mule accounts, freezing their accounts for two months or more is a disproportionate penalty. Also, the Court’s suggestion that unusual transactions must be automatically reported to the police and physically verified raises privacy concerns. These measures must ensure that genuine account holders are not penalised for bank failures. Many of these scams are run from compounds using trafficked Indians in conflict-ridden parts of Myanmar and in Cambodia and Laos where they have thrived due to some degree of official patronage. India must use its clout to pressure these regimes.
Editorial Context: Beyond gullibility: On digital arrest scams. This editorial examines the institutional, constitutional, and pragmatic dimensions shaping public policy and governance in India.

Any transaction of ₹1,000 or more that is ‘unusual’ for an account holder’s declared profile, or linked to a reported account, can be held for up to 60 days, and longer if directed by the police. In cases where small traders and Jan Dhan account holders have unknowingly received transfers from mule accounts, freezing their accounts for two months or more is a disproportionate penalty. Also, the Court’s suggestion that unusual transactions must be automatically reported to the police and physically verified raises privacy concerns. These measures must ensure that genuine account holders are not penalised for bank failures. Many of these scams are run from compounds using trafficked Indians in conflict-ridden parts of Myanmar and in Cambodia and Laos where they have thrived due to some degree of official patronage. India must use its clout to pressure these regimes.

articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: Social security concerns of unorganised sector workers remain

One year after the implementation of the Code on Social Security , the Union Labour Ministry has constituted the National Social Security Boards for Unorganised Workers and Gig and Platform Workers. The constitution of the boards, though delayed, is a welcome step. However, the highly centralised nature of this mechanism may hinder its optimal outcomes. By design, the Union Government controls both the Boards: they will be chaired by Union Minister for Labour Mansukh Mandaviya. The Board for Unorganised Sector Workers will have 40 members, nominated by the Union Government. They include seven members representing unorganised sector workers and seven members representing employers of the unorganised sector. Similarly, the Board for the welfare of gig and platform workers will have 22 members with five representatives each from the aggregators and the workers. But they have no significant representation of Central Trade Unions from the Opposition side or from the State Governments ruled by the Opposition. Labour is in the Concurrent List of the Constitution and both the States and the Union must work together to improve the living standards of workers.

The International Labour Organization defines social security as the ‘protection that a society provides to individuals and households to ensure access to health care and to guarantee income security, particularly in cases of old age, unemployment, sickness, invalidity, work injury, maternity or loss of a breadwinner’. The Union Government claims that the country’s social security coverage has increased from 19% in 2015 to 64.3% in 2025, which is around 94 crore citizens. However, it is apparent that the unorganised and gig and platform workers, who make up more than 92% of the country’s total workforce, are far from enjoying any social security under this definition. Almost two decades ago, the National Commission for Enterprises in the Unorganised Sector, headed by economist Arjun Sengupta, recommended a slew of measures to improve the social security of workers in the informal sector. The issues raised by the panel still remain unaddressed. A report prepared by Justice V. Gopala Gowda for the Keralam Government in March this year flagged certain anti-federal and anti-worker characteristics in the Social Security Code and suggested amendments. The Union Government should take the trade unions and the State Governments on board while creating new systems and mechanisms to address the social security concerns of the vast majority of workers.

articles.title: M.P. Police inspector mowed down by truck carrying illicit liquor in Dewas; racket supplying liquor to Gujarat uncovered
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: According to police, the liquor was being smuggled from Harda district to Gujarat; truck owner arrested, driver remains at large

An inspector of Madhya Pradesh Police was on Monday mowed down in Dewas district by a truck that he had intercepted on suspicion of smuggling illegal liquor, police said on Monday. The officer has been identified as Khategaon police station in-charge Dilip Puri.
An investigation launched following the incident has uncovered an illicit trade network spanning in multiple districts of Madhya Pradesh that supplies liquor to Gujarat.

According to the police, the incident took place around 1.30 a.m. on Indore-Betul highway when Mr. Puri was leading one of the four teams formed based on intelligence inputs that large amounts of illicit liquor was being transported from Harda district’s Timarni to Gujarat.
During the checking, a parked truck was spotted near Sandalpur in Dewas district and Mr. Puri had asked the driver to step down for a search.

“The driver, however, with the intent of killing Dilip Puri, ran him over with the truck and fled the scene. Mr. Puri died during treatment. The driver also tried to run over constable Sohan Jaat, who has suffered injuries,” an official police statement said.

The driver abandoned the truck after some distance and fled the scene. Dewas Superintendent of Police Aditya Mishra said that the truck was seized and more than 1,800 litres of illicit liquor in about 200 cartons were recovered from it. A video of the truck’s inspection showed that the cartons had been kept in a hidden chamber, made by laying down an additional metal surface to project the vehicle as empty.

Special Director General (DG) of Police Upendra Jain, who has been deputed by Chief Minister Mohan Yadav to oversee the probe, told The Hindu that the driver has been identified as Gajendra Rawat alias Akku, a resident of Alirajpur district, and a search is on for him. He said that the vehicle had been provided by Kairam Singh Changod, also from Alirajpur, and the local police has taken him into custody and is being questioned.
Mr. Jain said that a case under BNS Sections 103(1), 109(1), 121(2), 3(5) and Section 34(2) Madhya Pradesh Excise Act, 1915, has been lodged.
The Special DG said that the investigation has been revealed that the illicit liquor was being taken from Harda to Gujarat.

Mr. Jain said that the police have identified several people involved in the illicit liquor network. They are Patendra Jaiswal, a resident of Badwani district who owns a government licensed liquor shop in Harda, and his business partners — Manish Jaiswal of Indore, Mohin Jaiswal who lives in Gujarat, and Rahul Jaiswal of Harda’s Timarni and his associate Vijay Rao, a resident of Indore.
